questions.question: A grid has 8 equal squares: 4 squares across and 2 squares down. A line of symmetry runs straight down the middle, so the left half has 4 squares and the right half has 4 squares. On the left half, 3 squares are shaded. How many squares must be shaded on the right half so the whole grid has line symmetry?
questions.explain: A mirror image copies the same number of shaded squares onto the other side, so 3 shaded on the left means 3 shaded on the right. The trap is answering 6 — that is the total for the whole design, not the number on one half.

questions.question: A grid has 12 equal squares: 6 squares across and 2 squares down. The line of symmetry is horizontal, so the top row of 6 squares is mirrored by the bottom row of 6 squares. In the top row, 5 of the 6 squares are shaded. When the design is finished with line symmetry, how many squares are shaded in the whole grid?
questions.explain: Each shaded square in the top row needs a matching shaded square below it, so 5 + 5 = 10 squares are shaded altogether. A common slip is answering 5, which counts only one half of the finished design.

questions.question: A design is made on a strip of 6 equal squares in one row, numbered 1 to 6 from left to right. The line of symmetry is vertical and runs between square 3 and square 4. Square 2 is shaded. Which other square must be shaded to give the strip line symmetry?
questions.explain: Count how far the shaded square is from the line: square 2 is the 2nd square to the left, so its mirror is the 2nd square to the right, which is square 5. The trap is picking square 4, the square right beside the line, instead of counting equal distances.

questions.question: A grid has 20 equal squares: 4 squares across and 5 squares down. A vertical line of symmetry runs down the middle, giving a left half of 10 squares and a right half of 10 squares. On the left half, 7 squares are shaded and the rest are white. When the design is completed with line symmetry, how many squares in the whole grid are white?
questions.explain: The white squares get mirrored too: 10 - 7 = 3 white on the left, so 3 + 3 = 6 white in the whole design. The trap is answering 3, which is only the white squares on one half.

questions.question: Priya is making a mosaic on a grid 10 squares across and 4 squares down (40 equal squares) with a vertical line of symmetry down the middle, so each half has 20 squares. She has shaded 13 squares on the left half. On the right half she has already shaded 4 squares that are correct mirror images. How many more squares must she shade on the right half?
questions.explain: The right half needs 13 shaded squares in all to mirror the left, and 4 are already done, so 13 - 4 = 9 more. The trap is answering 13 and forgetting the 4 squares that are already shaded.

questions.question: A 4-by-4 grid has 16 equal squares. A design on it must have TWO lines of symmetry: one vertical down the middle and one horizontal across the middle. These two lines split the grid into four quarters of 4 squares each. In the top-left quarter, exactly 1 square is shaded. How many squares are shaded in the finished design?
questions.explain: Reflect the shaded square across the vertical line, then reflect both squares across the horizontal line, so 1 square becomes 4 — one in every quarter. The trap is answering 2, which uses only one of the two lines of symmetry.

questions.question: Ethan is planning a symmetric flag on a grid with columns numbered 1 to 8 from left to right and rows labelled A, B, C, D from top to bottom. The vertical line of symmetry runs between column 4 and column 5. The square in column 2, row C is shaded. Which square must also be shaded?
questions.explain: Reflecting across a vertical line keeps the row the same and only flips the column: column 2 is 3 columns left of the line, so its mirror is 3 columns right, which is column 7 in the same row C. The trap is changing the row as well, or landing on column 6 by counting one column short.

questions.question: Jasleen is tiling a wall design on a grid 6 squares across and 3 squares down (18 equal squares) with a vertical line of symmetry down the middle, so each half has 9 squares. She has placed 7 blue tiles on the left half and will mirror them on the right half. Blue tiles cost $2 each. What will all the blue tiles in the finished symmetric design cost?
questions.explain: First mirror the tiles: 7 + 7 = 14 blue tiles, then find the cost, 14 x $2 = $28. The trap is $14, which either forgets to mirror the half or stops after counting the tiles instead of multiplying by the price.

questions.question: Marcus is making a symmetric bookmark on a strip of 9 equal squares in one row, numbered 1 to 9 from left to right. The line of symmetry runs vertically straight down the MIDDLE of square 5, so square 5 is split in half by the line. Squares 3, 4 and 5 are shaded. When the design is finished with line symmetry, how many squares are shaded altogether?
questions.explain: Square 3 mirrors to square 7 and square 4 mirrors to square 6, but square 5 sits ON the line and is its own mirror, so the shaded squares are 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 — that is 5. The trap is answering 6 by doubling all three shaded squares and copying the middle one twice.

questions.question: Sofia is designing a quilt block on a 4-by-4 grid, with rows numbered 1 to 4 from top to bottom and columns 1 to 4 from left to right. Her line of symmetry is the DIAGONAL from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner, so folding along it makes the two triangle halves match. The square in row 1, column 3 is shaded. Which square must also be shaded?
questions.explain: Folding along the top-left to bottom-right diagonal swaps the row number and the column number, so row 1, column 3 lands on row 3, column 1. The trap is reflecting left-to-right as if the line were vertical, which keeps you stuck in row 1.

questions.question: Liam is completing a symmetric border on a strip of 8 equal squares numbered 1 to 8 from left to right, with a vertical line of symmetry between square 4 and square 5. Squares 1 and 3 are shaded on the left. Liam slides the pattern across and shades squares 5 and 7, saying it must be symmetric because two squares are shaded on each side. What should he shade instead?
questions.explain: A mirror image flips the order instead of sliding it: square 1 is 4 away from the line so it mirrors to square 8, and square 3 is 2 away so it mirrors to square 6. Matching only the NUMBER of shaded squares on each side is the classic trap — each square must sit the same distance from the line as its partner.

questions.question: Emma is making a symmetric window design on a grid 8 squares across and 6 squares down (48 equal squares) with a vertical line of symmetry down the middle, so each half has 24 squares. She shades 16 squares on the left half and will mirror them on the right half. She has 30 red stickers, one for each shaded square. Does she have enough stickers?
options: Yes, she will have 14 stickers left over
questions.explain: Mirror first: 16 + 16 = 32 shaded squares, then compare, 32 - 30 = 2 stickers short. The trap is comparing 30 with only the 16 squares on one half and thinking there are plenty left over.
